title: The bribed guards (Matthew 28:11–15)
hook: the guards are paid to tell a different story
tomorrow: the doubters were on the mountain too. what did Jesus say to them?

segments.voice: Yesterday two women ran from an empty tomb with fear and great joy, sent to go quickly and tell. They weren't the only ones leaving that garden in a hurry.
screen: `FEAR AND GREAT JOY.` → `WHO ELSE IS LEAVING?`

segments.voice: Two versions of the same night can be going around a group chat before breakfast. Matthew has that too. The women are still running toward the disciples when some of the soldiers who guarded the tomb walk into the city, to the chief priests, and report "all the things that were done." The quake. The stone rolled back. The same morning, the same news, carried in two directions. One group was told to go quickly and tell. Listen to what the other group is told to say.
screen: `TWO VERSIONS BEFORE BREAKFAST.` → `ALL THE THINGS THAT WERE DONE.` → `ONE MORNING, TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: The chief priests meet with the elders and give "large money unto the soldiers." With the money comes a script: "Say ye, His disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept." Some readers smile at the script itself: if you were asleep, how would you know who came? Then a promise of cover, if the governor hears of it: "we will persuade him, and secure you." And the soldiers' answer, in one plain line: "So they took the money, and did as they were taught." Did as they were taught. A story can be learned like lines in a play. Now follow the money through Matthew's last chapters. It began with Judas asking the priests what they would give him. Thirty pieces of silver. Now, at the other end, large money again, so a story will go one way and not another. Some readers hear bookends: silver to hand Jesus over, silver to explain the empty tomb away. One to tell a friend tonight: Matthew's Greek uses the same word, argyria, silver money, for both. And between them run two women who were paid nothing and carried the news anyway. Matthew doesn't comment. He sets the purchase beside the running women and leaves them side by side: a story you're paid to tell, and a story you'd tell for nothing.
screen: `LARGE MONEY UNTO THE SOLDIERS.` · `STOLE HIM AWAY WHILE WE SLEPT.` · `THEY DID AS THEY WERE TAUGHT.` · `SILVER AT BOTH ENDS.` · then, large: `TRUTH IS NOT FOR SALE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where a small untruth would be easier: a reason you give, a number you round, the version of a story you usually tell. Say the true version once, quietly, out loud, in a single sentence. Then let the breath settle, and notice what it would cost to say that sentence to the person who needs to hear it.
The bribed guards. Soldiers paid large money to say the body was stolen while they slept, and Matthew tells you so.
Carry this: truth is not for sale, even when the offer is large. Matthew, nearly done.

screen: `DAY 1485 COUNTS.` → `MATTHEW, READ THROUGH · 59 OF 60.` → `TOMORROW: THE DOUBTERS WERE ON THE MOUNTAIN TOO. WHAT DID JESUS SAY TO THEM?`

howItsDone: Some churches read Matthew 28 in the Easter season; this short scene of the guards and the money sits between the empty tomb and the mountain in Galilee.

myth: Matthew says the disciples stole the body
that's the story the soldiers were paid to tell. Matthew reports it as bought.
the soldiers turn the money down

the chief priests promise to handle the governor for the soldiers
if this come to the governor's ears, we will persuade him, and secure you.

fork.setup: you close at a café. the inspector asks if the fridge failed overnight. your manager hints there's a bonus if you say no. what's truth-not-for-sale here?
options: tell the inspector plainly what happened overnight.
say you weren't on shift, which is technically true.
take the bonus, then fix the fridge so no one's hurt.
fork.reveal: the guards learned a script for money, and Matthew names it as bought. a technically true dodge is still a script someone paid you to say.

original.note: Greek: silver pieces, money. the large money of Matthew 28:12, the same word as Judas' thirty pieces.

trapdoor: what you thought: a small detail before Matthew's big ending.
what it means: the guards are paid to tell a different story, and Matthew says plainly that it was bought.
what a scholar hears: argyria, silver money, in 28:12, the same word as Judas' thirty pieces in 26:15: bookends of bought words.
guess: soldiers paid to say the body was stolen
soldiers punished for sleeping on watch
soldiers who let a prisoner go for a fee
recall: a stone, a seal and a watch on the grave

chat.says: i forgot to book the community center for our last concert. Kayla says blame the office. tempting??
options: Tell Ms. Reyes it was you. The guards' story was bought; the truth isn't for sale.
Blaming the office is small. The guards' lie was about something much bigger.
Let Kayla say it, so you never lie. In Matthew, the guards did the talking.
chat.meaning: The soldiers took the money and did as they were taught, and Matthew calls it bought. The truth costs Grace something, but it isn't for sale.

chief priests.meaning: leaders of the temple in Jerusalem

elders.meaning: senior leaders who met with the chief priests

governor.meaning: Pilate, the Roman official who sentenced Jesus

argyria.meaning: Greek: silver money, pieces of silver

notes: Matthew 28:15 ends 'this saying is commonly reported among the Jews until this day'. The lesson leaves that clause out entirely so the scene can't be heard as blame on Jewish people. A Keeper should confirm.
'Some readers smile at the script itself' and the silver 'bookends' (26:15, 28:12) are offered as readings, not as Matthew's stated point.

'The quake. The stone rolled back.' recalls Matthew 28:2 (yesterday's reading), cited as paraphrase.
